These same gentlemen who want to abolish titles want also to banish appeals to the Privy Council, and if one talks privately with many of them, one will find they will state that the Governor General of Canada.

is a figurehead and costs a great deal of money to the country and ought to go. Time and again I have heard that stated, and it cannot be disputed, although some of them have not the courage to get up and say so. What other ties remain? We have simply the Crown and King left to bind us to the Motherland, and three legs having gone it will not be hard to knock out the fourth, and then we shall have the whole Empire tottering and coming down. In my judgment, every one of those ties, light as they are, is a silver thread that holds us to the Crown and to the Empire.
Believing that, I said in the committee, and I say here, that if any one is qualified to bestow distinctions and titles on soldier, sailor or civilian, it is His Majesty the King and his faithful advisers that surround the Throne. Having laid down that principle and having been defeated in the committee, I say I was perfectly consistent when I said, "If you do not take titles from His Majesty you shall not take them, with my consent, from any one else." We therefore moved- an extreme radical and myself working hand in hand-that "Honourable" and "Eight Honourable," not having come from the Throne, should also be banished. Strange to say, the gentlemen that said "We are out to pull up all titles by the roots and to banish every distinction," voted in retention of the appellations "Honourable" and "Eight Honourable," while we Imperialists voted for their abolition. Fine consistency, Mr. Speaker. Beautiful consistency. Surely the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMas-ter) can see that even he was getting somewhat out of hand with himself when he had to support the retention of "Honourable" and "Eight Honourable" and at the same time do away with all titles emanating from the King. Now, Mr. Speaker, seriously-
Hear, hear.

Well, if my hon.
friends do not think I am speaking seriously they may say "hear, hear." I have the commendation of my own conscience in the matter and have better proof of the correctness of my position than the applause of hon. gentlemen opposite, because when they applaud me I always think I am going wrong. I say that "Honourable" and "Eight Honourable" are the most disagreeable and most uncalled for of all the titles we have. Suppose you call me "Honourable" and I am not.entitled to the term; I have to come back and say I am not honourable. Then you say: "You are in the dishonourable 
class," and rightly so. Therefore, I say that the man who presumes to be called "Honourable" arrogates to himself certain characteristics of mind which require that he shall deal truly with his neighbour, that he shall not oppress the poor, that he shall not wrong his neighbour to the extent of a single dollar, and that he shall live an absolutely circumspect life. If he does not fulfil these obligations, he does not deserve the title "Honourable," for it carries within itself elements of character which none of the others have. A man might be a blackguard for all his title of "Honourable;" but the man who deserves the title must live up to all the attributes it implies. Therefore I believe we were absolutely consistent when we moved that the titles "Honourable " and '' Eight Honourable " should be abolished. But that was not all. We have heard some criticism of the last clause, which is about the only one I may be said to have fathered, and I will tell you why, Mr. Speaker. I think I was the mover of that in the Committee, and strange to say though I have been in a great minority most of the way through, even the Democrats swung round finally, when they were shamed into it, and voted for this. Would you believe, Mr. Speaker, that we had gentlemen upon that committee who, having held that His Majesty the King and his advisers should not bestow titles upon Canadians, had the wonderful audacity to get up there and tell us that though we would not accept titles from our own King whose advisers had no right to send them to Canada, yet we would take them from every other nation in Europe. What do you think of that, Mr. Speaker? Can hon. members cheer at that, or at the action of those gentlemen on the committee who, having said that no titles should come from the King at the head of the British Empire, were prepared nevertheless to take them from every European country? What does that indicate?
Disloyalty.

Yes, disloyalty and
worse than that.
Hear, hear.

Well, my friends
may think that I have nothing to support my arguments in this respect, but I have taken the precaution to fortify my position as to the consistency of the course that I have followed, and I have a document here that will prove to this House that I was absolutely consistent in what I did in this

matter. This is an order that I got this afternoon from the Department of External Affairs, from the hands of the titled gentleman whose honour is above reproach,-Sir Joseph Pope. It reads:
Regulations respecting Foreign Orders and Medals applicable to Persons in the Service of the Crown.
Orders.
1.	It is the King's wish that no subject of His Majesty in the Service of the Crown shall accept and wear the Insignia of any Foreign Order without having previously obtained His Majesty's permission to do so, signified either:
(a)	By Warrant under the Royal Sign-Manual, or
(b)	By private permission conveyed through His Majesty's Private Secretary.
2.	Permission given by Warrant under the Royal Sign-Manual will enable the Insignia of the Foreign Order to be worn at all times and without any restriction.
Private permission will only enable the Insignia to be worn on occasions specified in the terms of the letter from the King's Private Secretary conveying the Royal sanction.
3.	Full and unrestricted permission by Warrant under the Royal Sign-Manual is contemplated in the following cases:-
For a Decoration conferred-
On an Officer in His Majesty's Naval or Military Forces lent to a Foreign Government; on an Officer in His Majesty's Naval or Military Forces attached by his Government to a Foreign Navy or Army during hostilities; or on any British Official lent to a Foreign Government and not in receipt of any emoluments from British public funds during the period of such loan.
In the case of decorations awarded in recognition of services under the Red Cross, permission will only be granted where such services have been rendered in a war in which the Empire has itself been engaged, and by persons serving under one of the officially recognised British voluntary aid societies of under similar societies of Allied States duly recognised by the Government of those States.
4.	Private or restricted permission is contemplated for Decorations which have been conferred in recognition of personal attention to the Head of a Foreign State, and which are therefore of a more or less complimentary character, and will, as a rule, only be given on exceptional occasions when in the public interest and for political reasons it is deemed expedient that the acceptance of a Foreign Decoration should not be declined. Private permission will generally be given jji the following cases:-
For a Decoration conferred-
(1)	On British Ambassadors or Ministers abroad when the King pays a State visit to the country to which they are accredited;
(Note.-A State visit is defined as one on which the King is accompanied by a Minister or High Official in attendance.)
(2)	On Members of Deputations of British Regiment's to Foreign Heads of States;
(3)	On Members of Special Missions when the King is represented, at a Foreign Coronation, Wedding, or Funeral; or on any Diplomatic Representative when specially accredited to represent His Majesty on such occasions; and such Members of his Staff who actually attend the ceremonies in their official capacity ;
(4)	On Naval and Military Attaches only after completion of five years' service at the post to which they are appointed in that capacity.
(5)	Private or restricted permission will not be given to-
(1)	British Ambassadors or Ministers abroad: when leaving;
(2)	Members of British Missions announcing the Accession of a Sovereign;
(3 British Officers attending Foreign Manoeuvres ;
(4) Naval Officers of British Squadrons visiting Foreign Waters.
There is considerably more, but I think I have read enough to show that foreign titles are not to be recognized in this country without the permission of His Majesty* by special request. I see my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) smiles at this. He probably is wearing his decoration without that permission because it may have been bestowed before this order was made. But this document which I have just received from the Department of External Affairs absolutely defines the procedure, and I believe that the Privy Council has the right to decide, when a foreign title is bestowed upon any citizen of Canada, whether or not he shall wear it. If there were no such provision what would be the situation? We have been having a war, though, judging from the amount of attention we are devoting to such trivial matters as the question now under discussion, one would hardly credit the fact. These foreign titles are coming into Canada, and I as a Britisher was amazed to find that on that committee there were men who would support the practice of accepting foreign titles after having denied their own King the right to bestow British titles on Canadians. I was astounded at a proposition of that kind. The hon. member shakes his head, but what I say is quite true.

I rise to a point of order. The hon. member is making remarks in reference to members who were appointed on the committee. That has absolutely nothing to do with the amendment, which is to refer the subject back to the committee.

I have tried to bring up my family in the same direction. I take no credit to myself, it was due to the soundness of my bringing up; I was fed on oatmeal porridge and the Bible, and in my early days I was brought up to work, and I worked as hard, I believe, as any man of my age in this House can say he worked at that time. Therefore, I knew the dignity of labour and I do not despise the workingman. I am a democrat of the democrats when it comes to meeting the workingman, and I am not

I tell you, gentlemen, and I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that your duty to-night is to see to it that His Majesty the King is not insulted by any such rubbish as is contained in this report; and I hope you will send it back to the committee with instructions to amend it and to intimate to some of the democrats who sit in that committee that you expect, whether the report they bring in goes to the King or not, that such report shall be worthy of the dignity of a committee of this House and worthy of the subject they undertake to legislate upon, and not make- I was going to say foolish men of hon. members here who, I believe, have in them some wisdom as well. I hope that the course I am now advocating will be followed and that the men responsible for this report will be taught that this is not the kind of thing that will make for the dignity of this House or for the uplifting of the democracy of this country. I have much pleasure, Mr. Speaker, in supporting the amendment of the hon. member for East Algoma.

Mr. Speaker, in August, 1789, when the Three Estates met in Paris it was proposed by one of the members that the titles given to the French nobility and borne by them at that time should be abolished. One speaker got up and made a speech in support of titles, and the privileges of the French nobility, and was as eloquent and as vigorous as the hon. gentleman who has just spoken. I refer to L'Abbe .Maury. He was then the man who sang in the French constituent assembly the [DOT]swan song of the titles given to the nobility of France; and I think Mr. Speaker, that I can say to-night, without being mistaken, that the hon. gentleman (Mr. iCockshutt) has sung the same song for titles in Canada. I admire the hon. gentleman; I admire the vigour with which he expresses

himself, and I admire the robustness of his Toryism; but unfortunately he represents a period which is passing. I was astonished to hear the hon. gentleman talk as he did about the hon. member for Kingston, and to heat him declare that the latter's motives may have been tainted with disloyalty. In making that statement I think the hon. gentleman was carried away by the warmth of his sentiments. He, surely, does not believe that any man in this House could be moved by feelings or sentiments of disloyalty.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. I think the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) has mistaken my observations. If I applied any such words as he attributes to me to the member for Kingston, I beg to apologize to that hon. gentleman; I certainly had no such intention. I was making a general remark, and I applied it to nobody as far as I know.

I was sure it was only necessary to draw the hon. gentleman's attention to the expressions he used to elicit from him the apology that any gentleman would give to the House and to the hon. member referred to.
I was also surprised to notice that the hon. gentleman omitted from his speech a very important feature of this question, and failed to give us his views on it. What will become of the titles actually borne by the bishops of the Anglican church? According to this report, if I understand it correctly, the archbishops and the bishops of the Anglican church will be deprived of their titles if the report passes. Is that the intention of the gentlemen who composed the committee which sat on this question and made this report to the House? Before casting my vote I would like an answer on that point. I am quite sure, Mr. Speaker, that the Anglican bishop of Toronto would be very much surprised if this report is adopted, to find himself debarred from using a title which gives him a distinction over a Methodist minister. I think this is a very important feature of the question and one which should be considered very seriously by the members of the House before they record their votes.
Both the hon. members for East Algoma and Brantford declared they were very much surprised to see that upon the conclusion of the war, when the people of Canada have serious problems to face, this Government has not brought forward enough legislation to keep members busy, and that the House has already discussed upon three occasions

during the present session the very useless question of titles. Not very long ago, Mr. Speaker, a question of great moment to the people of Canada was introduced here, namely, the question of dealing with our Canadian railways. I can state without any fear of contradiction that the discussion on that question lasted not half as long as the discussion on the present subject, nevertheless, the Government, through the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen) invoked the closure against the Opposition. Why should we be allowed to discuss matters of this kind and waste the time of the country while the Government sits there merely listening? I will tell you the reason: it is that the Government is not ready to undertake the problems that await a solution;, the Government is not ready to bring down a solution of the reconstruction problems that is demanded; and it would rather have the House discuss questions of this kind than tell us what it intends doing to see that Canada is made a great and united country as it should be. I may be told by hon. gentlemen opposite that the discussion has been long because this question is a very difficult one to solve, and has many aspects and many sides. Mr. Speaker, I am inclined to think that is true, judging by the many sides that several members opposite have taken on this question; and before I cast my vote I would like to be sure that the gentleman who moved the adoption of this report will not vote against it.
I wish to call the attention of the Government to another matter, Mr. Speaker. I think that the moment is ill chosen to ask the representatives of the people to discuss a question of this kind. To-day we know the situation all over^Canada. We hear the cry of discontent coming from the Prairie Provinces; we know the situation that exists in Winnipeg; we know that Canada is on the brink of revolution-and the Government does nothing.
-Some hon. MEMBERS:	No, no.

And the Government asks us to discuss- a question of this kind. Mr. Speaker, I think the sooner this Parliament gets down to real business the better, for discussions of the character we have had to-day tend to aggravate the people rather than to content them.
On the merits of this question: Am I in favour or against titles?-my answer is very simple. I am a plain, -simple, ordinary Liberal, and I am against titles. I will tell you why.

I think that titles and distinctions in many cases have been nothing but a bait to the cupidity of people, a screen to their infamy at times, and a reward for their servility. The hon. member for Brantford has mentioned the situation which exists in England. I admire the British nobility. It has given throughout the centuries examples of devotion and of self-sacrifice that no other class of people have ever equalled. But, Mr. Speaker, I say that these English people have so borne themselves not because they are dukes, or earls or viscounts, but because they are British people and.
_ nothing else.
But if we study the history of the nobility all over Europe what do we find? Take, for example, the noble families of France. If you go back to the origin of many of those families you will find that their titles were obtained very often because the founder was nothing more than the illegitimate son of a king. Turning to England, take the great family of Churchill-a family of which every Britisher is proud. The founder of that family obtained his title on account of the infamy of his sister. Mr. Speaker, those are historical facts. Titles have been used in that way throughout the history of the world, and should we keep them here in Canada?
How and why are titles given here in Canada? The last Emperor of Brazil, Bom Pedro, was a very clever man. In his memoirs he tells u/ that he had to build a hospital in his capital of Bio, but the Government did not have the necessary funds, so he decided to try the following plan. He sent out a statement to the effect that people who subscribed a certain amount would have their names inscribed in letters of gold on the front wall of the hospital; that the people who subscribed a lesser amount would have their names inscribed in letters of silver; and that the people who subscribed a still lesser amount would have their names inscribed in letters of bronze. When the hospital was built through the money thus obtained, Dom Pedro had the names inscribed, and' above he added this sentence: "This monument has been erected to charity through human vanity."
Well, we have before us to-night a monument erected by the Premier of this country, not through the charity of our country, but through the vanity of man. This monument, which we call the Borden Government, is a government that has been bought-that has been built through the vanity of its members. The builders who
have contributed the bigger amounts of money will see on the front wall in letters of gold their names, such as those of Sir Joseph Flavelle and Sir Clifford Sifton; the names of people who have done less, but also have done quite a lot, will appear in letters of silver, such as those of Hon. Mr. Calder and Hon. Mr. Rowell; and in letters of brass will be seen the names of Hon. Mr. Blondin and Hon. Mr. Sevigny; and, Mr. Speaker, in letters of chalk, so that they may not remain very long, will be seen the names of Hon. Mr. Crerar and Hon. Mr. Carvell.
I do not wish to detain the House any longer. I admire the convictions of people like the hon. member for Bradford. They stand for the old institutions, for what was very noble. They stand, like the noble people in the French Constituent Assembly, who fought for their king although he was to die. But although we admire these people we have got to combat them, because their ideas are away behind the times. I am in favour of progress, I am in favour of Liberalism, and I think, Mr. Speaker, that the abolition of titles will bring a better state of things in our Canada that we all love.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to discuss this subject upon its merits. Having accepted the honour of a title, I feel debarred, as I stated when the matter was before the House on the last occasion, from taking any active part in the discussion. I desire, however, to state the position of the Government on the motion now before the House.
For two sessions this subject has engaged the attention of this Parliament. Prior to the' assembling of this session the Prime Minister requested that the matter be referred to a special committee of the House so that a deliberate and reasoned judgment of the committee and of the House might be had. When the House met the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. N'ckle) placed his motion upon the Order Paper. I saw him about it, informed him of the request which the Prime Minister had made, and I asked if he would be willing that his motion should he referred to a special committee of the House in order that it might have full consideration, with a view later to discussion in the House, and such action as it might be thought desirable for the House to take. He stated that he would consult with some of those who were especially interested in the matter and inform me whether or not he would

agree. Later, after giving the matter consideration the hon. member consented to my suggestion, with the result that when his motion, which was that of a private member, was before the House I moved that it be referred to a special committee. I say that in explanation because some reflections have been without warrant cast upon the hon. member for Kingston by reason, as has been alleged, of his changing his vote. He did not change his vote, Mr. Speaker, he carried out honourably his undertaking with me. The disposition of the motion was entirely in accord with parliamentary practice, and it was perfectly open to my hon. friend to agree to it. I make that statement in justice to the hon. member for Kingston.
I desire to say this with regard to the position of the 'Government: This motion does not involve a question upon which the Government has any pronounced policy, as I stated when the matter was last before the House. The Government, therefore-I desire to make this perfectly clear-makes no request to any members supporting it with respect to the matter; it is perfectly open to each member here, so far as the Government is concerned, to vote as he may see fit. The same remark applies to members of the Government. This is a matter upon which members of the House, and members of the Government themselves, may hold different views, and as it is not a question of policy it is the desire of the Government that the House should express its view freely upon this question-which, notwithstanding what has been suggested by some hon. gentlemen who have spoken to-day, 'is one of considerable importance. The member for Kingston has brought the question forward for two sessions. His speeches leave no room for doubt as'to his earnestness in the matter. It is fairly before the House, and what the Government desires is a frank expression of opinion upon it.
The hon. member for Kingston stated this afternoon that I had requested him to have the report of the Committee submitted to the House at as early a date as possible. That is true, and the Government is willing to assume the responsibility of this matter now being before the House. It was my belief that it could best be dealt with in the first instance by a committee which would consider it in all its aspects. The Committee chosen was one which commanded the entire confidence of the Hohse, and I feel that I should express to all the members of that Committee my thanks for the attention which they gave to the subject and for

their promptness in bringing it down for final action.'
I have stated that I feel rather debarred from discussing this matter upon its merits by reason of the fact that I have had the honour of having a title bestowed upon me. I feel very much disposed to agree with much of what the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) said this afternoon; there was a great deal of sound common sense in what he said. My own view is that this matter has assumed a disproportionate importance. It is an important question, but I do not believe it is so important, either intrinsically or in the eyes of the public, as the debates in this Parliament would' indicate. However, each hon. member is to judge for himself as to that. The chances are that if the academic or abstract question was put to, any body of citizens in Canada, or elsewhere for that matter: "Are you in favour of titular distinctions?" the answer would be "No." But I submit that is not a fair test. The question is, what would the answer be if the matter could be fully discussed and considered with and by those people? It seems to me that the real test that should be applied by the House of Commons is this: What is in the public interest? So far as individuals are concerned, they need not be considered. Whether this or that or the other citizen receives a title is of minor consequence; the true principle upon which this House should proceed is: What is in the national interest? Is it wise that titular distinctions and all that they imply should be abolished? My own view is that there is not and should not be objection to the principle of titular distinctions; but I do believe that the circumstances surrounding their bestowal are of utmost importance. I think that in all the British-speaking countries the bestowal has been on. altogether too generous a scale and has not proceeded upon the principle that it should have proceeded.
I believe that if the question of bestowal had received more careful consideration in the past by all Governments in Canada, this question would not be before us to-night.
I am not going over the ground which has been so ably traversed this afternoon with respect to the propriety and advantage of distinctions. But I submit this: There are men in this country, and in other countries of the Empire-in fact, in all the countries of the world-who give very distinguished and very valuable public service without reward, in the money sense, such as comes to those who attain success in other callings.

I do not say that to those men a knighthood would be an incentive. To the best of them,
I do	not	believe it	would; to	someof them it	might. I	do not believe	that	men	who serve	the State	putforth	their	effort with	any idea	that
they are to be rewarded by a title. On the other hand, I do believe that men who have put forth effort of the greatest advantage to the public, who have served the State for long years-the Prime Ministers of this country, for example-should receive some distinction as a mark of the State's appreciation of their advices. Take the Prime Ministers of this country. Take Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and a Provincial Premier, such as Sir Oliver Mowat. If the question had been submitted to the people whether these men should be deprived of their titles, there would have been an overwhelming vote in favour of their being allowed to retain them; the people would say: These men are entitled to have their public'services marked by the conferring of titular distinction upon them. Appreciation encourages men. I do not believe that men who serve the State-men such as those I have mentioned-are at all inspired to effort by any hope of titular distinction.
But I do believe they are encouraged to go on in their work by the conferring upon them of a .distinction which marks the appreciation of their services to the State. After all, men are only boys grown up. As has been pointed out to-day, at school, and in college, and on the battlefield, and in campaigns, there is no doubt that prizes are looked upon as rewards and do stimulate to effort. More than that, they encourage further effort. Personally I fail to see the distinction which is made between the awarding of prizes, military medals or other decorations to soldiers and distinctions to men in public life or in some other walks to which I shall refer a little later on.
I would ask the Acting Prime Minister if this does not involve the question of precedence and, therefore, become a class distinction and not a decoration.

I will come to that just in a moment. Who will say that the Cross of the Legion of Honour has not always powerfully appealed to the French soldier, to inspire and to stimulate him to effort? Who will say that the Victoria Cross has not powerfully appealed to British and Canadian soldiers? The principle of conferring distinctions for action that is unselfish, that is altruistic, that is for the benefit of the people, is a sound one. I am the first to admit the very great difficulty in the matter of bestowal of titles and, as I stated before, I think it has been the unwise, too wide bestowal of titles and particularly the conferring (bf hereditary titles that has caused this question to be more or less of an issue in this House. But in public life, and also in the world of science, of literature, and of philanthropy, it is very much in the national interest that some means should be open to the Government-because the responsibility belongs to the Government-to mark the nation's sense of appreciation of distinguished service rendered in those fields, and if the bestowal of titles could be confined to that class. I do not believe the people would raise any objection. It has been put forward here that many distinguished citizens of Canada have been offered and have refused titles, but that does not necessarily lead to the conclusion that titles should not be granted. It is open to any citizen in this country to refuse any title offered to him. As the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) suggested this afternoon, it is a matter of the point of view, and I am sure many gentlemen who have refused titles would not necessarily take the view that the principle of the bestowal of titles is unsound.
With regard to hereditary titles, I have no hesitation whatever in saying that I concur in the report of the committee, but I have grave doubt whether, from the standpoint of national interest, this report as it stands to-day should be adopted by this House. I am speaking, not as leader of the House in the absence of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), but simply as a member of Parliament expressing my individual View, and I do not desire to be taken as .speaking in any other capacity. My view is that the report of the committee as it stands is too sweeping, I think the Prime Minister of Canada advanced the matter as far as it should be advanced when he caused the Order in Council to be passed, which was brought down last session and which has been referred to in this debate. That is my individual view, and that is all I desire to say at the present time to the House

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this question before the vote is taken. Before, however, referring to the

question under consideration, I want to enter an emphatic protest against an expression used by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) who spoke before the acting Prime Minister. In referring to the troubles in Winnipeg and other parts of the country, he said that this Dominion was on the brink of revolution. That is going entirely too far, and I do not think the actual circumstances in any respect warrant such a statement as that. It is perfectly true that a very large body of men are on strike in the city of Winnipeg from which I come, and it is also true that some very unreliable, untruthful and improper reports have been sent from that city by way, I think, of the United States. Emphatic denials have come with regard to the reports, and we learn, from Government sources, that the situation is thoroughly in hand; that the constituted authorities are in command, and that the situation is steadily solving itself, so that I do not think the country need be unduly excited over the situation as it exists either in Winnipeg or in any other portions of the Dominion.
With regard to the subject under consideration, I think that too much emphasis has been laid upon the point that a great deal of the time of this Parliament has been consumed in the discussion of this question. It is perfectly true that last session we occupied considerable time in discussing the matter in Parliament, and during the present session we have also spent some time, but I dissent from the view that it was entirely misspent time. If the Prime Minister of this country had taken the position that the Acting Prime Minister has taken this session, the question would have been disposed of in perhaps two or three hours, and I believe it would have been satisfactorily disposed of, because the House was almost unanimously opposed to the granting of titles. Put the Prime Minister who had the question under consideration with the home authorities staked the existence of the Government on the issue, and many of us on this side of the House, although we were very much in earnest in regard to the abolition of titles, felt it would be undesirable that the country should be plunged into a parliamentary crisis on a question of perhaps subordinate importance, at least, a question that could wait for solution until a later time. That was the reason why the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle), myself and some others declined to take

the responsibility of overthrowing the Government on the question of titles.
Then the question came up at the present session, and the resolution was again introduced by the hon. member for Kingston as it was introduced by the same hon. member last session. Last session I moved as an amendment to his resolution, which dealt only with hereditary titles, that all titles should be extinguished. At this session, when the hon. member for Kingston introduced his resolution, he adopted my amendment of last session which provided for the abolition of all titles, inclusive of hereditary titles. I had given some study to the question, and I came to the conclusion that there might be a constitutional difficulty so far as the British authorities were concerned if the few hereditary titles that exist in the Dominion at the present time were extinguished or if an attempt were made to extinguish them immediately.
So I conceived the idea of moving an amendment at the present session that these titles should expire with the death of the holders. That amendment has been implemented or embodied in the resolution of the committee that is before the House to-night, and that is the method that is being adopted. The Acting Prime Minister when he referred to the hon. member for Kingston as having agreed to allow his motion this session to stand until the matter might be inquired into by a committee, might also have stated, had he thought of it, that he discussed the matter with myself before the vote was taken and indicated to me the course that he, as Acting Prime Minister, purposed to take. The hon. Acting Prime Minister nods his head, in acknowledgment of the accuracy of my statement. I decided to follow the lead of the hon. member for Kingston, and naturally came in for a considerable amount of criticism from a few of my " friends "-if I may be permitted to put the word in quotation marks-and when I rose to vote in the House I was jeered at by certain members of the Opposition. However, on the principle that he laughs best who laughs last, I felt I could afford to endure the con-temptable sneers from a few insignificant characters, if in the end the object that we *who are opposed to titles had in view, was attained. I could not help feeling that although the matter could have been summarily disposed of, the fact that it should be referred to a special committee which would make a thorough inquiry, might, after all, furnish a stronger reason in the minds of the masses for the adoption of such a

report as is embodied in that before the House to-night. I have no particular reason to change my view in regard' to that.
I want for a moment to call attention to the report itself, because there are some members of this House who some days or weeks ago were in favour of abolishing all titles, and in two or three cases they have now expressed some doubt because they were persuaded by the eloquence of our good friend the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Sheard?. En passant I must say how greatly I enjoyed the oration which he delivered this afternoon. It was wonderfully dramatic and in some respects moving, but it had, in my judgment, very little bearing upon the real issue. He tells of certain worthy people who received distinction at the hand of the King-if you call it a distinction-by being knighted. But the point that we who are opposing titles in this House have in mind is that while it might, >as the hon. leader of the Government said, be excused in certain cases, it has been so scandalously misused in Canada as to become an offence in the nostrils of the people. And I want to say to any of my good friends who may think of voting against this report of the committee, that they had better pause and consider the effect of their vote, not necessarily on their political position, but on the country at large. The country on the whole is deeply disturbed, and perhaps that is quite natural following so great a wax as we have just passed through. But times have changed, in my judgment; and however much the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) or other hon. members may deplore the fact, a change has come over the spirit of the dreams of the people of this Dominion, and the democracy is not only being ushered in, but it is in fact ushered in. And in my opinion such a step as we propose to-night could not fail to be effective in appeasing this uneasy public opinion. The abolition of these social distinctions could not fail to have a beneficial effect. Now, let me for a moment, for the purpose of putting the question fairly before any weak brethren-if I may be allowed to use that expression-read what the report actually says, because I think there may be a misapprehension on the part of some members, who, as I said, were probably over-persuaded by the eloquence of the hon. member for South Toronto. Paragraph (a) reads:
(a) To refrain hereafter from conferring any title of honour or titular distinction upon any of your subjects domiciled or ordinarily resident in Canada, save such appellations as are of
a professional or vocational character or which appertain to an office.
That paragraph means the extinction of knighthoods, C.M.G.'s, and O.B.'s. C.M. G.'s and C.B.'s are merely steps in the ladder to knighthood, and in coming to the decision which it reached, the committee only aimed at extinguishing such titles as placed a prefix to the name of the recipient, and we felt that if we voted against the conferring of knighthoods we ought also to abolish C.M.G.'s and C.B.'s, and made a clean job of it. That is the object of that paragraph. I need not discuss the paragraph with regard to the abolition of hereditary titles, because the House seems to be unanimously agreed that they must go. My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) and my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) waxed, I think, unduly eloquent, or perhaps unduly warm would be a more accurate description. They indulged in statements of much more warmth than one would expect from either of them with regard to the alleged titles of " Right Honourable " and " Honourable," and the statement was made that the members of the committee were to be censured for not recommending the abolition of those two distinctions.	"
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend
from Brantford says, " Hear, hear," so he agrees with my statement of the case. According to my recollection of the situation-and I would like hon. gentlemen to particularly note the point-the reason we did not touch the distinctions " Honourable " and " Right Honourable " was that these are authorized by the British North America Act, and are conferred by virtue of a provision in that Act. So that the committee, and indeed this Parliament, would have no power to deal with them, and the House will agree with me that it .was particularly desirable that we should refrain from recommending the abolition of these two particular appellations. Paragraph (4) says:
Tour committee, however, do not recommend the discontinuance of the practice of awarding military or naval decorations, such as the Victoria Cross, Military Medal, Military Cross, Conspicuous Service Cross, and similar decorations to persons in military or naval services of Canada for exceptional valour and devotion to duty.
I want the House to be particularly clear with regard to the position of the committee in this connection. We refrained .absolutely from interfering in shape, form o.r manner with military distinctions and
27.34

decorations which might be conferred for valour upon the field. We had before us the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Griesbach) who gave the committee very valuable information. He addressed the House this afternoon and it is possible that he left the impression that the committee had not been as fair with the military profession as it should have been. However, I want to assure the House that [DOT]the committee was scrupulously careful not to interfere in the slightest degree with the conferring of distinctions upon naval and military men. That will relieve the committee from any blame or censure in .this respect. I want to deal with the question of foreign titles, to which my friend the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. .Cockshutt) referred to a few moments ago, I shall not say with eloquence, but rather with undue heat, and I believe that even he will agree with me, as I am sure the members of the House will, that he did not present the case with perfect accuracy, when II state the facts as they are. Let me first read the clause of the report dealing with that matter.
Tour committee further recommends that appropriate action be taken by legislation or otherwise to provide that hereafter no person domiciled or ordinarily resident In Canada shall accept, enjoy or use any title of honour or titular distinction hereafter conferred by a foreign ruler or government. I
I may explain how that came about. The committee had no warrant to deal with the matter of foreign titles. It had come before the Cabinet in a certain manner and they referred the question to our committee for a decision. There were a number of members of the committee who, like myself, felt that inasmuch as the reference of the particular questions to the committee did not embody that point the committee should not deal with it. I was one that took that ground, and after some discussion the matter was ruled upon by the chairman of the committee. The hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) thought it came within the jurisdiction of a committee appointed to make a general finding and be so ruled.
The hon. member for Brantford indicated with great warmth that the members of the Committee were actually in favour of foreign titles being received by Canadians. I want to absolutely dissent from that statement, and I think in doing so I shall be borne out by all the members of the Committee. Excepting himself, there was not, according to my recollection, one single member-I see the hon, member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thom-

son) agrees with me-of that Committee who took the view that foreign titles should be received intq this country. It was merely a question as to whether or not we should deal with the matter. The position taken by the hon. member for Brantford entirely falls in that regard.
There was an amendment moved by the hon, member for Qu'Ap-pelle and afterwards we were asked to get together, which we did, and we framed the resolution which was passed.
I want to say that the statement made by the hon. member for Springfield is absolutely correct- that there was no member of the Committee expressed himself as in favour of continuing foreign titles.
You moved an amendment.
I did.

I do not wish to suggest that the hon, member for Brantford desired to deliberately misrepresent the case, but he got carried away with the sound of his own voice and the enthusiasm of the moment, and I think he consequently misrepresented the position of the committee. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson) will make >a statement later and I am sure he will endorse my description of what bajipened at the committee. The hon. member for Brantford told us here with great enthusiasm that he had got from the Under Secretary of State this afternoon a statement that Parliament had nothing to do with foreign titles, anyway, and that no one in Canada could receive or wear a foreign title Without the permission of the King. If that be so there can be no possible objection to that particular clause in the report being adopted. Anyway, it leaves the matter to the Government to deal with in some proper manner later on, If the permission of the King must be received to accept or wear a foreign title, we need not worry very much about the existence of that clause in the report.
What I want to impress upon hon. members is that the report embodies nothing but what has been generally accepted at one time or another by the majority of the members of this House since the question was brought before it last session, and during the present session. Under the report hereditary titles are to be extinguished on the death of the holders, and knighthoods are to cease from the present time.

The hon. member for Brantford spoke of the insult that was offered to the King by addressing him in the manner proposed in the report. As a matter of fact, the King has really no responsibility, although he finally "does the trick," in connection with these titles. The recommendations for titles are made by the Prime Minister of the day. No doubt the whips and the corporations may have considerable influence on the Government of the day in reference to the conferring of titles. But the King should not be charged with the responsibility. This is the only way that this House has of putting an end to what we regard as an improper practice, as a practice which has led to very much heartburning throughout the country and which, I believe, is not in the general interest of the public, a belief which I am convinced is shared by the great mass of the people of the country. The members of the House should have clearly in their minds the point upon which they are voting when they come to record their votes in a few minutes. Members need not worry at all about foreign titles when the King is the supreme authority in that regard. The committee only made a finding in regard to it because the matter was referred to it by the Government. We have absolutely guarded the military ranks in this country. The two things we have done are, first, to recommend the ending of hereditary titles and, second, 'to recommend the ending of knighthoods. That is practically all that the members are asked to vote upon.
I think that this country owes a considerable debt to the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) for his courage and pluck in bringing this question before Parliament and for the ability and care which he has displayed in presenting the case on the different occasions that it has been brought up in this House. I resent the reflection of the hon, member for Brantford, although he has explained it, in saying that there was something disloyal behind this attempt to wipe out titles in this country. Doubtless there are many little crosscurrents in evidence, but I do not think there is anything sinister behind this movement against titles; I am quite sure that the hon. member for Kingston, who sent two of as brave boys as this country has produced overseas to fight the battles of Canada in the great war, is not influenced by any sinister or improper motives. On the contrary, I think the hon. gentleman interprets the feeling of the country very clearly with regard to this question. It may be that many members think that we
have devoted too much time to its consideration, to the exclusion of other matters which they regard as of greater importance.
I repeat, however, that it is a question that means a great deal to the people of this country, and in the long run I believe that if titles are abolished, as this report proposes, we shall have done a good day's work for Canada, and the time which has been devoted to it will not have been spent in vain.	.
I have a great deal of sympathy with the position of the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham), who said that members who regard this question lightly will probably discover that they have made a great mistake when they come to discuss it with their constituents, and when they find what the real feeling actually is throughout the country with regard to it. T believe that is a fair statement of the situation. While the people are not perhaps especially excited, still I believe that if this issue could be referred by a plebiscite, uninfluenced by other considerations, to the entire population of Canada, it would be carried by the enormous majority of twenty, thirty, or fifty to one, because people generally, I reiterate, are sick of the institution of titles and the manner in which they have been misused by the governments of the day since Confederation.
There is one other point to which I wish to refer before resuming my seat. I read a letter in the press the other day, and I want to give a brief extract from it to the House. The writer says:
What chanoe is there outside of an aristocracy for the development of the following virtues: Modesty, truthfulness, sincerity, regard for the-feelings of other people, genuineness-what chance has any one of them in the fierce competitive struggle of democracy? Not the smallest. They get choked out-stifled in the crowd, killed.
Proof-take our Toronto or Montreal crowds -a necessity. We Canadians-born believe that a nation-not a mob, but a nation-should have-one part of its population in which such things can be preserved.
I shall not enumerate the list, but I invite the House to recall and scrutinize the galaxy which holds the doubtful honour. I would not like to be understood as saying: an offensive word against the gentlemen as a class who enjoy the doubtful distinction, as there are undoubtedly some excellent and deserving men upon the list. Hon. gentlemen, however, no -doubt recall the reasons for which many of the decorations were conferred by the governments of the day.

If the virtues of -modesty, truth, sincerity and tenderness are to be found only in the ranks of our belted knights, and especially if these virtues which should be universal are mostly confined to that limited and interesting collection of citizens, then I think, with all earnestness, we should invite you, Mr. Speaker, when at the opening of each session, you invoke the Almighty to save the King, to also implore the Deity to include the country as well.
In Canada titles have not been generally distributed because of the possession of the qualities of genius, or because of any distinguished service to the country but largely because of political services rendered to this or that party or corporation, whose conduct may have been glaringly inimical to the best interests of the people.

I shall not occupy more than one or two minutes in discussing this matter, and I would not take that much time were it not for the fact that it so happened I was not present, when the debate occurred last year on this matter, nor was I in attendance when the debate took place on a former occasion during the present session. The hon. members for Springfield and Brome paid very high tributes to the hon-. member for Kingston for his courage in bringing this matter ito the attention of the House. I would not for one moment wish to be understood as reflecting in any way on the courage of that hon. gentleman; but if the statements made by the three hon. gentlemen referred to are correct, that eighty or ninety per cent of public sentiment is in favour of the motion moved by -the hon. member for Kingston, the thought occurs to me that it requires little courage to move such a motion, but it does require some courage to express opposition to it. The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) in the course of his remarks intimated that it would be a grave mistake for this House not to pass this report because of the effect it might have on the prevailing situation as indicated, for instance, in- the city of Winnipeg, and that it would add if anything to the unrest which is exhibited in that city at the present time. I happen to have in my hand a -clipping from the Winnipeg Free Press. That clipping gives an account of a meeting held by the Great War Veterans in Winnipeg, and I quote in answer to the statement made by the hon. member for Springfield, an- expression of opinion by one

of the Veterans, named Captain Wheeler, who said in reference to titles:
" What do we care about titles," declared the speaker, " what we want is a chance to live pro-perly and to know that we can be able to buy food for our wives and children at the lowest possible price."
Apparently, if we are to take the words of -that gentleman as any guide, the people of Winnipeg are not very much concerned about the question of titles. Furthermore, I express my own opinion, which, of course, may be. wrong, when I say that I think there is very little concern in the country with regard to this whole matter; I think the people generally are very little -concerned about the question of titles.
I do believe that opinion throughout the country as in this House is practically unanimous in regard to hereditary titles; but I do, think there is a difference of opinion in regard to the granting of other titles. Personally, I do not believe in the granting of these titles at -all, and in so far as Canada is concerned, I think we can get along very well without them. But they have been conferred upon men in this country,-some of whom have been mentioned by previous speakers, and I rather incline to the view that the public generally were pleased rather than otherwise, not that the title of "Sir" was conferred upon John. A. Macdonald oi Wilfrid Laur-ier, but that the head of the British Empire took a means of signifying his appreciation of the services of men of that type. But titles have been conferred rather promiscuously, and I cannot shut my eyes to the fact that the wealth of the individual apparently has had a good deal to do with the -matter, -although there are notable instances in this country of titles having been conferred on men who are not by any means wealthy.
I think the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) expressed the situation very well indeed; at least, my view coincides with his. It has been stated, and this is one of the -things that appeals to me, that the King does not confer these Canadian titles except on the recommendation of the Prime Minister of Canada. If that is true, why not address the opinion of this House to the Government of this country? Why address it in the form of a demand to be placed before the King? Is it that the House believes that an expression of opinion addressed to the Prime Minister would be ignored by him? I do not believe for one moment that the Prime Minister would ignore the opinion of this

House addressed to him in the words of the motion asking for the adoption of this report; and if he did not ignore such expression of opinion, there would be no recommendations made to the King asking for titles to be conferred on Canadians resident in Canada, and consequently no titles would be conferred.
After all, there are two parties to this question; there is the party here in Canada, and the party over in the Old Country. There are different sentiments in the two countries. I feel inclined to respect the sentiments of the people in the Old Country, although I do not agree with their views in regard to titles. But, while I am willing to vote for any resolution expressing the opinion of this House as against the granting of hereditary titles or titles of knighthood, I do not think we should go beyond that and place our opinions in the form of a demand that the King should take this or that action. I have the greatest respect for those who hold a different view in regard to the matter. If it comes to a vote I am going to vote against the adoption of the report for the reason I have stated. My opinion may be misrepresented, and there may be some who will say that I am in favour of the continuance of titles in this country. Very well; I am willing to take my chances in regard to that, notwithstanding the remarks of some bon. members that it was as much as one's political life was worth to take that course.
I repeat, Sir, that in my view we should be perfectly within our rights in expressing the opinion of this House that it was in conformity with the sentiments of the people of Canada that hereditary titles should not continue to be conferred on Canadians resident ir. Canada. I believe that such an expression of opinion would get us just as much as we would obtain by placing a demand before the King and saying: " We want you to do thus and so." That seems to me to be a rather harsh way of treating the matter.
Distinctions have been made even in the resolution. I know, of course, that many object that it is undemocratic to have certain men ;n this country who are known as " Sir This " or " Sir That." I do not approve of it myself. But if they want to play with that sort of a trinket, why, all right; I do not think the public cares very much about it one way or the other. But if it is improper and undemocratic that I should address a gentleman in this country-who has had a knighthood conferred upon him- as Sir,-and really I cannot treat him courteously unless I so address him-then is it democratic for my friends, the hon. member for Kingston and the hon. member for Brorne-both lawyers-when they go into the court room bowing and scraping to the gentleman on the bench to say, " May it please you lordship" or "Your worship this " or " Your worship that," or " Your honour this " or " Your honour that?" Of course, to suggest that that is undemocratic, or that it is undemocratic to refer to the dignitaries of some churches as " My Lord Bishop," I suppose, would be carrying democracy a little bit too far. But to be perfectly consistent, I cannot see why one should object to my speaking to John Jones-if he has been knighted-as " Sir John," if it is proper to refer to a judge on the bench as " Your lordship."
Nor do I think that it is altogether consistent that we should make no effort to do away with the titles of " Honourable " and " Bight Honourable." Of course, it is true that those are titles which may come to some honourable gentlemen in this House, if they reach the height of their ambitions, -and no doubt they are worthy of holding those titles-and we would be lacking in courtesy if we did not address them as " Honourable " or " Right Honourable."
I repeat, Sir, that I believe the sentiment of Canada is opposed to the granting of titles; but I think we will be going as far as we should go in taking action on this .matter in this House if we give expression to that opinion and carry our request to the Prime Minister or to the Government.

speakeroldname: Hon. F. B. CARVELL (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not much sympathy with the contention, which has been made a number of times this evening, that time has been wasted in the discussion of this matter in the House. I have always had the idea that the people elect representatives to come to Parliament and to take whatever time may be necessary for the discussion of matters that come before them. If the Government was criticised during the lasit session of Parliament for one thing more than another, it was on the ground that sufficient time was not given for the discussion of matters which many members wanted to discuss. I took the ground this year that Parliament should be called as early as possible and should sit as long as members wanted to sit and should discuss matters 'of public interest affecting the people.
I am rather inclined to agree with the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) that there is not the demand for the abolition

27,'58

of titles in Canada that some people think there is; still, I do believe that if the proposal were put to a vote it would carry by a large majority. I believe that the sentiment of Canada is against the conferring or retention of these titles. I a<m opposed to them-not, perhaps, from the standpoint taken by some hon. members, but as a matter of principle. I do not believe that the aristocracy of Great Britain during the last thousand years has been the advantage to the country that some people have tried to make it out to have been. One had only to go to Great Britain before the war-and the condition would be much exaggerated since the war-to see the great gulf that existed between the classes and the masses. What has been the origin of all the social revolutions that have taken place in Great Britain since the repeal of the Corn Laws if it has not been the fight between the classes and the masses; if it has not been the fact that the aristocracy were arrogating to themselves rights and powers and privileges which were considered by the common people as inimical to their best interests, and taking to themselves rights which the common people believed they were being deprived of? The principle upon which I shall vote on this question is this: I do not want to see that condition of affairs built up in Canada. It has been admitted here by all sides-I am not blaming one political party more than another-it has been admitted by the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White), that there has been an abuse in connection with the granting of these titles during recent years. Many men have received them who, perhaps, are not entitled to them; and were it not for that abuse, I assume that this matter would not be under discussion to-night.- Personally, I have no objection to a man receiving a distinction from his sovereign who had become a great inventor or a great scientist, had contributed something to the uplifting of the world, had been honoured by being made Prime Minister of his country, or something of that kind, because in nearly all these cases the distinction would be actually conferred by the sovereign or by the ruling power as a reward for what the recipients of the honours had done. But we might as well get down to the ordinary condition of affairs and realize that where there was one of that class there would be a dozen whom the King did not know at all and about whom he cared nothing. The King has nothing to say about it, except in these few outstanding cases. People are made knights 
because they want to be made knights; because they have sufficient influence with their political friends, or in some other way. After all, Mr. Speaker, the recommendation for the creation of a knighthood in Canada comes from the Prime Minister, from the Government.
In all cases?

Yes, I think in all cases, although there may be some outstanding exceptions. I have no doubt that Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the present Prime Minister, after being elevated to the Premiership, received their titles direct from the King. But in the great majority of cases it is the building up of an aristocracy because people want to become the aristocracy; and that is the principle I am opposed to.
In a sense, I am sorry to see the matter before the House in the shape it is. It has created a good deal of feeling; there has been a good deal of discussion about it. I was afraid, on coming into the Chamber just before six o'clock-I had not been able to listen to all the debate-that in some way the report of the special committee, if adopted, would ask the King to refrain from granting military distinctions. I listened to the member for Edmonton, and immediately got a copy of the report and read it over; but I saw nothing in it to bear out that contention. Evidently the committee deliberately avoided expressing any opinion derogatory to the granting of military decorations; and that is as it should be. They have asked the King-and that is only the manner of asking, because really the request goes to the Government of Canada; they have asked the powers that have the right to recommend these distinctions to refrain from granting hereditary titles. That everybody agrees with. Secondly, they have asked them to refrain from granting ordinary knighthoods1-about that there seems to be some difference of opinion. I have no feeling against any gentlemen who have accepted titles in the past, or who might accept them in the future, because that is largely a matter of individual opinion. But holding the views that I do, believing that the creation of a privileged class is not in the best interests of a country like Canada, and having regard to the fact that the question is before Parliament for the expression of its opinion, I intend to vote against the amendment and for the adoption of the report of the Special Committee.

Mr. Speaker, I would not have taken up any

of the time of the House had it not been for the rather serious reflections and insinuations made by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) against the other members of the Special Committee. I felt, as the hon, member was speaking, that he was rather telling tales out of school that might better have been kept quiet. However, I would not have minded had the statements been correct. In referring to other members of the Committee and to those who were opposed to him, tire hon. gentleman used the term " disloyalty " over and over again. He apologized so far as the member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) was concerned, but he evidently still considers the rest of us as disloyal-and every other person who opposes him on the question.

I do not think the hon. gentleman is justified in making that statement. 1 pointed out that there were four threads that held us to the Empire and that the cutting of those was an element of disloyalty. If the hon. gentleman did not cut any of the threads 'he certainly does not come in that class.

The hon. gentleman has no right whatever to impute disloyalty to me, even if I did believe in all the things he says'-which I do not. He has no more right to impute disloyalty to me than I have to impute disloyalty to him because he holds an opposite opinion. This talk about disloyalty is getting threadbare; it is a shame that that cry should be used in this House in connection with the discussion of any question that comes before it. Any cause which has to be supported by talk about disloyalty is a pretty weak cause; it is only because of the weakness of the cause'my hon. friend supports to-night that he uses that cry.
The hon. gentleman tried to leave the impression with the House that the members of the Committee who were opposed to him on most questions that came before the Committee were in favour of those foreign titles being received. Not a word was said in the Committee that would justify that statement. In support of his statement, he says that I moved an amendment. I did move an amendment, which the hon. gentleman himself accepted and put into his motion. If you saw his motion here you would consider it unworkable-a rather strange looking motion. I do not think he would care very much to quote it himself.

Has the hon. member got it?
I74i
Mr. L. THOMiSON: My hon. friend was very willing to accept it. We were told that this resolution which we proposed to submit was an insult to His Majesty. It was a resolution [DOT] addressed to His Majesty asking him to refrain hereafter from conferring any title of honour or titular distinction and so on, but my hon. friend says he supports the amendment which provides that we ask His Majesty or demand of His Majesty:
To provide that appropriate action be taken by legislation or otherwise to ensure the extinction of an hereditary title of honour or titular distinction, dignity or title, as a peer of the realm, on the death of a person domi -ciled or ordinarily resident in Canada at present in enjoyment of an hereditary title of honour or titular distinction, dignity or title as a peer of the realm, and that thereafter no such title of honour, titular distinction, dignity or title as a peer of the realm, shall be accepted, enjoyed or used by any personand so on. It is a tremendous insult to His Majesty to say: We do not want you to confer knighthoods, but it is all right to say: You must not confer peerages on Canadian citizens. It just shows how hopeless a case my hon. friend has when he brings forward such absurd arguments. One thing is undignified and insulting, while another thing, absolutely the same, if not a little worse, is all right. I do not propose discussing -this question, because it has been pretty fully discussed. Like the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) I do not know that there is a tremendous agitation in regard to this matter, but notwithstanding that, I believe the general public think that we should act. I am not saying that I believe a lot of time has been wasted in this House, and I do not purpose wasting any time myself, although I have noticed that the members who spoke most about wasting time took up a good deal more of the time of the House than they needed to do, and I do noP intend following their example. I am following rather along the line of what the Minister of Public Works said, and the reasons given by him are my reasons, and for those reasons, I purpose voting against the amendment and for the resolution.
Hon. NEWTON W. ROWELL (President of the Council): Mr. Speaker, I wish to make just one or two observations before the vote is taken. The question of hereditary titles is not open for discussion at the present time; that question was settled more than a year ago. The Order in Council which was passed by the Government and submitted to the House expressly set forth that no hereditary title of honour

shall hereafter be conferred upon a subject of His Majesty ordinarily resident in Canada, and further provides that :
Appropriate action shall be taken, whether by legislation or otherwise, to provide that after a prescribed period no title of honour held by a subject of His Majesty now or hereafter ordinarily resident in Canada shall be recognised as having hereditary effect.
That Order in Council sets forth the most advanced position which any Government in this country had, up to that time, taken on the question of titles in Canada. Those provisions were approved by the House, and that decision has been communicated to the Imperial Government, so that both Government and Parliament are committed to that policy in relation to hereditary titles, and I am sure that appeals to the judgment of the people of Canada.
Referring to the question of knighthoods, while there may not be the same unanimity as there is on the question of hereditary titles, I believe the overwhelming mass of the people of Canada have reached the conclusion that it is not in the interest of the country as a whole that further titles of knighthood should be conferred. I think they have reached that conclusion on very sound grounds. The Minister of Public Works and other hon. members have already spoken on the subject, and I shall not repeat their arguments. I do not believe it is consistent with the democratic conditions prevailing in a country like Canada that we should continue to mark in this way certain men, no matter how honourable, no matter what distinguished service they render; for experience has shown us that we cannot limit it to the few men whom every one would recognize as properly entitled to be so marked. From our* experience, I believe we must reach the conclusion that it would be wise to discontinue that policy in the future. I listened with great interest to it'he hon. member for Edmonton West, and if I understood him aright he pointed out that under the report as printed it would interfere with the conferring of military distinction. If that is true, I should like to see the report amended so that it would not interfere with conferring any distinctions, decorations or titles upon men who had served in the present war, my reason being that large numbers have already been so recognized, and further, I know of some who have been recommended for recognition. The matter came before the Government some time ago, before this House met, and the Government wisely and properly declined to take

action until this question had been considered by a Committee of the Whole House. Personally, I cannot see why military men who have already received recognition should stand in a better position than those who have earned but have not yet received such recognition. Some may say: No military men should receive recognition. All I am suggesting is that they should all receive the same consideration. I must vote against the amendment because it says that we should continue to confer knighthoods on citizens of this country. I should be glad to vote for an amendment that would refer the report back to the committee to amend it so as to make it clear that it would not interfere with recognizing men who have served in this war and would pat those men in the same position as those who have already received recognition, tout if no such amendment is proposed I shall vote for the report.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queens):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to offer a
few words, not of argument, but rather of explanation. I was a member of the committee appointed to consider this question, and as I was not able to concur in the report, perhaps it is not objectionable that I should offer a few words of explanation why I was not able to agree with my colleagues. On the question of hereditary titles there is practically no difference between us, and I take it to be the view of this country and of this House that, neither on the recommendation of the Government or without it, and neither on the recommendation of the Prime Minister or without it, so far as this House has any influence, shall any hereditary title be given in Canada hereafter. I take that to be the meaning of the report, and on that I presume there is no difference of opinion.
Coming now to the question of titles generally, I have assented to the views of the majority on that question, but not without some hesitation and reluctance. I do not concur in the views of my hon. friends who claim that as a matter of principle the granting of these titles is wrong. In the earlier years of Confederation, in the years before Confederation, when honours of this character were granted tout seldom, and always granted to men of undoubted distinction, there was no public opinion against them. Nobody found fault with the conferring of honour, say for example, on Sir John A. Macdonald or Sir George Etienne Cartier, although I believe in tlhe beginning there was a little cause for

jealousy and trouble. It is historically known that when Mr. John A. Macdonald received his knighthood Mr. George Etienne Cartier was offered a minor honour, 2nd that this caused trouble and jealousy and an uncomfortable situation. Mr. Cartier resented it and Mr. Cartier's friends resented "it more freely. In the end Mr. Cartier received a consolation of a higher prize, in the form of a baronetcy, than that received by Mr. Macdonald. The authorities had ascertained that Mr. Cartier was not blessed with a son and that, therefore, the title would not last long. Beyond a little jealousy of that character I do not think there was any manifestation of public opinion against the granting of these honours so long as they were granted rarely and for services of undoubted merit.
It is only when in later years-and I am not speaking now of one party or the other-these honours were offered in greater abundance that any question began to arise concerning them. I think if we look over the list from A to Z, of the men who have been honoured with knighthood there will be found the names of a great many gentlemen of eminence and of long public service, men of distinction, with the recognition of whose merits no one can find fault. Indeed, nearly all on the list will be found to be honourable and estimable men. But when you ask yourself the question, why was this or the other particular man honoured, you find yourself in a quandary. True, some one who is honoured may be an honourable man; but there are thousands of honourable men all around him in the community. True, he is estimable, but there are estimable men in his neighbourhood in the same line of business, and of equal distinction, who receive no honour. As time went on and these conditions continued, there began to develop an opinion against knighthoods. It will be said with some force that the abuse of anything i$ no valid reason why you should abolish it; but the opponents of knighthood have argued with equally great .force that if the system should continue the evils will coexist with it; because if the appointments are made by the Government or on the recommendations of the government of the day it is inevitable that they will be characterized by favouritism of some kind, political or personal. These considerations, I think, have led to a considerable volume of public opinion against these honours. I do not think the country is at all excited about the matter, as some hon. gentlemen seem to think, but there is considerable
public opinion against it, and for that reason with some reluctance, and not as a matter of principle, I have concurred in the view that, as respects knighthoods,- an adverse recommendation should be made. If I could have an opportunity of voting on these matters separately, if there were submitted a question concerning hereditary titles, I should undoubtedly vote/against such titles, but I shall not have that opportunity. And if I could have the opportunity of voting distinctly on the question as it relates to ordinary knighthoods, I should with some reluctance vote against those titles. But 1 shall not have that opportunity either. Now, why did I differ from the committee? I thought that whatever public opinion there was in the country-and I am not magnifying it-had relation to hereditary honour and what is called ordinary knighthood. Public opinion did not concern itself with anything beyond that; why then should we do so? Why should we worry over C.M.G.'s, C.B.'s, and I.S.O.'s, which no one in the world except very few knows the meaning of? I doubt whether very many ordinary men know the significance of " C.M.G." It is a badge of honour and distinction, but five out of six men in the street, generally speaking, could not tell you what O.M.G. and C.B. meant. And if it pleased His Majesty in the ordinary course to make somebody a C.M.G. or a C.B. I see no reason why we should break our hearts over the fact.
