It may be that these two honours, C.M.G. and C.B. are steps in the order of knighthood, one in the Order of the Bath, and the other in the Order of St. Michael and St. George, and I suppose that if these orders generally were marked with disapproval, these minor honours would also be regarded with disfavour. But I do not see why w.e should worry about-it. Then there is the I.S.O.-The Imperial Service Order-given sometimes to old public servants. I could not tell you all who have it in Ottawa, but it never hurt any one. I do not see why minor honours should have entered into consideration at all.
Now we come to foreign titles and decorations. I was not present in the committee during all the proceedings, and during my absence some [DOT] resolutions were reached which I did not concur in. But very naturally and properly they were carried into the report of the committee. If it suits any foreign authority to grant a mark of distinction to any citizen of Canada, which distinction does not carry with it the title

of knighthood, I do not see why in the world we need object. These honours come seldom, being most frequent in the case of the French Republic, and a number of our fellow-citizens have had conferred upon them the Legion of Honour. I do not think we should seek to prevent any one from receiving such an honour if it pleases the French authorities to offer it and the recipient to accept it. Whatever public opinion there was on the subject was confined to hereditary titles and knighthoods, which involved the prefix, " Sir." Beyond that I do not see that there was any demand, and I do not think there was any need for the committee to present to the House a report concerning these things. The committee reported according to their judgment, and I am not finding fault with them. I am merely stating my own views. And inasmuch as I believe that there was no need for a consideration of these minor honours, I cannot agree in that, and I dissent from their report.

Mr. Speaker, I was a member of that committee and voted in support of the various resolutions which form the report now 'before the House. I have not changed my mind and shall vote in favour of the adoption of the report. It is not the time or the place ito split hairs, Mr. Speaker. The committee by a very large majority adopted the report. I think there were only three members opposed to the broad principle embodied in it, and the last speaker was not one of them. The committee adopted the report after a full discussion oh the matter, and the principle which was at stake was whether or not in Canada we should put an end for the future to any class distinctions. The committee almost unanimously decided that we should do away with all attempts at maintaining in this country any class distinction whatever. Sir, we are not living in Great) Britain. If we were, I would understand that perhaps members of the House might have some diffidence in the matter. There they have a different civilization and a different tradition as regards these distinctions. For my part, I wish to pay my respects to the British nobility. I know what has been the role of that nobility in history and how well it has behaved during the recent war. But, as I say, we are not in Britain; we live in Canada, in a democracy, and at the present hour, in view of what is taking place in the country, I do not know that Parlia-
ment could do better than abolish all *class distinction. Some hon. gentlemen have spoken about military decorations.
I am not opposed, Mr. Speaker, to military distinctions, such as the V.C., D.S.O., or the Military Cross,but I am of the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mir. Manion) that if you are going to give decorations to the higher officer you are creating again an invidious distinction between that officer and the modest, unassuming private who went over the top. The private is as much entitled in this war to any decorations, any distinctions as the higher officer.

I never said a word
about decorations; I said knighthoods.

Sir, in this war the private was a knight, in my judgment, as much as a colonel, the major, or the general. They were all knights and if you make a distinction, ll say that the greatest knights of all are the dead. Where are the decorations for the dead? Wooden crosses! Reference has been made by the hon. the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and he made it with that chivalrous spirit which generally inspires his thoughts and actions in this House and outside of it. As a matter of history, it is well that we should know how it came that my late leader became iSir Wilfrid Laurier. It is of record that in the campaign which preceded the election of 1896, at a meeting held in Ontario, Sir Wilfrid Laurier made the famous declaration; " I am a democrat to the hilt." After he became Prime Minister, the Queen's Jubilee took place in England and he was deputed as the representative of Canada on that occasion. He had not altered his views; he had not changed; he was, as ever, a democrat to the hil{. But how could he refuse the honour, the distinction, when, without being consulted, on taking his seat at Windsor Castle, as one of His Majesty's Privy Councillors he found his title in front of him. That is the history of Sir Wilfrid Laurier's knighthood. If he had been consulted he never would have accepted it, but if on the other hand he had refused on that occasion it would have been looked upon as a lack of courtesy on his part. But, as we all know, he was a grand gentleman. The manner in which the honour was conferred upon him on that occasion reflected his modesty, his true chivalry, and at the same time his devotion to the interests of 'Canada. But let me give here another instance from

Sir Wilfrid Laurier's career. It may throw light on what look place on the occasion to which I have, just referred. It will show, Mr. Speaker, that Sir Wilfrid Laurier always was a democrat .to the hilt in the sense he meant when he made that declaration prior to 1896. It is not known to the members of this House, it is not known to the public, but in the history of Sir Wilfrid Laurier which is being written at the present time, it will be made public. On one occasion, perhaps on two, but certainly on one, Sir Wilfrid Laurier was offered a peerage and he declined it. That was the spirit of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. The true democrats of this country can well look up to him as a guide.
I do not intend to say anything more on the subject. The problems that confront us are very serious indeed. I do not know that it is wise policy on the part of this or any ..Government to make a last-ditch fight for the maintenance of those titles which in the past have been so lavishly distributed. I have in my mind some titles which were given not very long ago and which shocked the public conscience, titles given to men who had no right and no claim to them. I am positive they were given without His Majesty knowing anything about them. They were the gift of the whips of the parties; that is all. They were given to these men because of some consideration. It has been stated publicly in England over the signature of responsible parties that titles were offered before general elections for a consideration. Why should we perpetuate that system in this young country of ours? Public opinion is absolutely opposed to any class distinctions in Canada, and the people will hail the result of the vote that we take on this question to-night.

Mr. Speaker, the amendment which I submitted was drafted hurriedly. I have another here the phraseology of which is a little better. 1 do not know whether I will be permitted to substitute it. It does not change the principle of the amendment in ahy sense.
No, no.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There is an amendment before the House and it is technically in order. What the hon. member asks is that he may put the same substance in better form. That can only be done with the unanimous consent of the House. I will read the altered form of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for East Algoma:
That the report he not now concurred in, but that it be referred back to the Special Committee with instructions to amend the same by striking out paragraph (a) of the proposed Address to His Majesty, and by striking out all the paragraphs after the said proposed address, and by adding the following paragraph to the report of the said Special Committee:-
" That in making recommendations to His Majesty for the conferring of knighthoods or other titular distinctions upon persons domiciled or ordinarily resident in Canada the greatest care should be exercised in the selection of the persons recommended, and that special regard should be paid to the personal merit and the distinguished services of the said person."
Is it the pleasure of the House that the hon. member shall have permission to substitute this for the amendment proposed?

If no other hon. member desires to speak, I should like to exercise my privilege of closing the debate. I may say that this afternoon I have found myself in the position in which Mr. Storey, later Judge Storey, found himself after he had been appointed to the Supreme Court bench. In his earlier years he had drafted an Act of Congress that was considered by him as a model of perfection. He felt assured that no matter what attacks were made upon it, it was impossible that ambiguity would arise in reference to the legislation of which he had been the author. But in later years when he had risen to the Supreme Court Bench, cunning lawyers, in arguing certain questions before him as being applicable to the Act that he had drafted, so confused him that he said that he hardly understood what his own legislation meant, and he found himself almost unable to interpret 'it. That is very much the position in which I would find myself to-day if I were to lend myself to the cunning arguments which have been submitted against the report. They have attacked it from every point, from the point of view of logic in this way, from the point,of view of logic in another way; they have criticised it on the grpund of loyalty and they have criticised it on the ground of inconsistency.
I would not care at this late hour to say very much in reference to the attacks that have been made, but I do not think, in justice to myself, that I can allow a personal remark which was made by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) to pass unnoticed. lit was a remark that cast the imputation upon me of having been inconsistent in my conduct and vote in this House on the 14th of last month.
The hon. the leader of the Government (Sir Thomas White) has certainly been most courteous in giving to this House an explanation of what occurred, and I may say that the explanation given by him is correct in every detail. When I introduced

the resolution into the House at the first of the session it remained on the Order Paper for a somewhat protracted period until my attention wias drawn to it by the Government. A few weeks prior to the discussion, the acting leader of the Government asked me if I would be prepared to take a fair, non-partisan and representative committee which would consider and discuss in a judicial manner the involved and difficult points covered by the resolution. I told him that such a committee would be acceptable to me. I explained the position to those who were supporting my motion and I had their concurrence in the arrangement.
I was amazed the night the debate took place on the 14th of April, when suddenly a political situation developed, and I found myself confronted with this difficulty: I had to take a position that certainly would be construed by the country as being inconsistent, or I had to break my word to the leader of the Government; and there are some things that a man of honour, even *when faced with the likelihood of severe criticism, must consider, more particularly when the breaking of his word would mean the breaking of a Government. I had pledged my word, and those who were behind me had pledged their word, that we would accept that committee. Men had left this House and gone to their homes for their vacation-the Easter vacation I think it was -believing that a committee was to be accepted; and it would have been the rankest perfidy, the rankest treachery on my part, if, when I found the Government of this country in a precarious position, I had not kept my word to a man whom I had known for twenty years and who in all that time never in the slightest tittle deviated from that which he had promised me. That is my explanation of the vote I gave that night. I used the wrong word in saying the word "explanation." It is not an explanation; it is a reason for the vote I gave that night. I had told the right hon. leader of the Government that I would accept that committee, and I had told many men who spoke to me in reference to the matter and had asked me if there would be a vote, that the matter would be referred to a committee; and would finally be discussed in this House free from being considered as a party question.
I would like to know why it was, under those circumstances, that the resolution was introduced in the way it was, and why in it the committee was not recommended?

The resolution had been
on the Order Paper for some seven or eight weeks. That length of time elapsed, if hon. gentlemen will remember, before the resolution was debated. I had simply to take it as it was*, before I was permitted to know what the conclusion of the Government was. Then the offer of a committee was extended to me and I accepted it as a fair solution of the difficulty. It may have been badly managed, I am not making any defence in regard to that; I am simply endeavouring to make it clear to the House that the Acting Prime Minister kept his faith with me, and I kept my faith with him.
You did not intimate in any way that there was such an arrangement.
I am not saying for one moment that certain gentlemen did 'not find themselves in an awkward position; not for one moment am I arguing that.
You did not care.

Yes, I did care. I do
not know what* riding the hon. gentleman represents who said I did not care. I oared more than most men think, and I would never have spoken if the matter had not been brought up in this House to-day-my lips would have been sealed.
Now, Sir, I want to direct the attention of the House not to a personal matter, but to the issue which is before us. The hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Sheard) spoke this afternoon with marked eloquence -an eloquence which shook the House, and shook the argument that I had advanced in favour of the resolution that I had introduced. It was a remarkable effort. But was the hon. gentleman consistent? He- waxed most eloquent in criticising the language in which the report was drafted. He said the language was an insult to His Majesty. He shook with vigour, and with. feeling, as he denounced the arrogance, if I might use the word, that prompted the Committee to say that His Majesty should be approached to provide that appropriate action be taken by legislation or otherwise, to ensure the extinction of titles. The hon. member for Brantford (Mir. Cockshutt) shook with similar indignation this afternoon when he approached the subject in the same way; and the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) trembled with indignation as he approached the matter from the same point of view. In imagination I could see His Majesty

shrinking back as this terrific and terrifying resolution was presented to him for consideration, and I said to myself as these gentlemen spoke; "Oh, consistency, thou art a jewel." Because I remembered that in 1918, on May 21st, the right hon. leader of the Government moved his amendment to my then resolution and the very gentlemen, who shook wiith indignation this afternoon and evening, voted for exactly the same' language that the Prime Minister put in his motion as the language that I put in the resolution which I submitted this afternoon. The resolution of the Prime Minister which carried in this House in 1918 read thus :
We, Tour Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the House of Commons of Canada, in Parliament assembled, humbly petition Your Majesty, praying that Your Majesty hereafter may be graciously pleased to refrain from conferring any titles upon your subjects domiciled or living in Canada.
And so on, and so on. The division took place on that resolution, and is recorded at page 2448 of Hansard, and among the names recorded in favour of that resolution I see the names of Edwards, Cock-shutt, and Sheard. When I drafted this report-because my hand was known in the drafting of it-I used the very language that the Prime Minister used so that an imputation could not be cast upon me in this House that I had acted in a disloyal manner. Because I have heard, not only in this House but outside, that there was an element of disloyalty in approaching His Majesty and asking that a certain concession be made that the Canadian people wanted. Where is the disloyalty in making any such approach? Is the monarchic institution so weak that it cannot stand by virtue of its worth? Do the hon. gentlemen who have spoken in this House want the House and the country to understand that the attachment between Canada and the Empire is so weak that it cannot be preserved except by the maintenance of titles of distinction? I do not believe it. I do not think this country believes it, and I do not think the members of this House believe it. Five hundred thousand men did not go to the Front and sixty thousand of them do not lie in Flanders fields because they hoped to win distinction; they went to the war because they were moved by patriotism; they went to the war called by a sense of duty. And I say it is an insult to the memory of those men to say that titular distinctions is the tie that binds the Dominion to Great Britain. Titular distinctions probably have no effect in binding the Dominions to the Motherland; but it is that warm bond of sympathy, the sentimental tie, that unites the Empire that covers all the seas and has made it so strong in the face of a mighty foe.
I want to say a word or two more. I want to say a word or two in reference to something the member for Bed Deer (Mr. Clark) said this afternoon. He is a magnificent debater. The flow of his language, the vigour of his intellect, the rhythm of his sentences, carries you along in a majestic flow. But what did he say this afternoon in the House? Not content with his marked abilities, not content with being the premier debater of this House, he used this afternoon in reference to me these words, and I did not rise to my feet at that time because I could hardly believe my senses when I heard the member for Bed Deer speak as he did.
He said:
X cannot, the way my mind is framed, concur in anything which is the embodiment at once of democratic cant and illogical nonsense. We are asked to concur In this report and recommend in one paragraph His Majesty to abolish all titular distinctions in Canada and retain the titles Honourable and Right Honourable, which I contend by any fair interpretation of the English language are themselves titular distinctions.
"Democratic cant"! Am I not to be regarded as being as sincere in advocating the abolition of titles as the hon.. member for Bed Deer is to be thought sincere in maintaining ithe position that free trade would be a sound economic principle for this ' country to adopt? If I cannot get all I want in. one bite, am I to be thought any more insincere than, he because the Government may give him something, but possibly not all he wants? Does he not realize that no well-matured policy, no great advance in public affairs is made by jumps? Progress is made little by little in any great reform; and I say to the members of the House to-night who are asked to vote for the amendmenJt of the hon. member for East Algoma that a subterfuge is being cast about the issue. It is not a question of whether this thing or that thing, in reference to logic, shall be the determining factor. The question is, shall this House or shall it not stand for what the people of this country want? The people of this country do not want titles continued. The hon. member for Frontenac has said that they do not want them continued, yet he shrinks back in horror from the vote. Why?

Because he thinks His Majesty may be insulted. And yet last year he voted for a resolution couched in exactly the same terms. The member for Bed Deer says that it is illogical nonsense. There never was a more logical committee than the committee that sat to deal with titles, .honours and distinctions. Let u 4 draw the veil aside and see what happened. The committee met and there was no question as to hereditary titles and their extinction; on that we were agreed. The next point was in reference to knighthood; on that the vote was 17 to 3, if I remember correctly. The next vote was on the minor classes of orders, and there the difference in the vote was not quite so marked-I do not know exactly what the vote was. The committee adjourned, and at the next meeting the hon. member for Red Deer raised the question that the titles " Honourable " and " Bight Honourable " should go if we were to be consistent. I said to him, " If you believe that, put it in the form of a resolution, and submit it to the committee, and let the committee vote upon it." The hon. member for Red Deer did put it in writing, and this is his resolution:
Mr. Clark moved : That this committee is of opinion that in case Parliament finds it expedient to abolish titles in Canada, steirs must necessarily be taken to see that no citizen of Canada resident in Canada wears henceforth the prefix [DOT] Honourable " or " Right Honourable."
What happened ? If the committee had accepted that they might have gone outside the reference, for the reason that the prefixes " Honourable " and " Right Honourable " did not form part of the subject matters that had been particularly discussed in the House. But if the committee had accepted that amendment I have no doubt whatever that the members who were opposed to the action the committee had taken on knighthood and the orders would have steadily pressed, and pressed, and pressed, one resolution after the other until they had reduced the whole thing to an absurdity. It would not have made any difference where you drew the line. No matter where it was drawn, imputations of being illogical and absurd would have been cast upon the committee. The committee were extremely logical. They said: " The subject matters that were before the House and the country were hereditary titles, knighthoods and the various classes of the Orders, and that is as far as we are going to go in the matter. And there they stopped. Therefore I submit, Sir, to you and to this House that there was nothing illogical in the action

of the 'Committee in voting on the question of the titles of " Honourable " and " Right Honourable."
Will my hon. friend permit me to ask a simple question? Is the term " Right Honourable " before a man's name a title?

I should certainly consider it a title. Now, another question has been raised, and by the member for Brantford (Mr. Coekshutt), who was also a member of the Committee. I must admit (that I am a little lost in following his argument. He sltarts out with a burst of eloquence, stating that the King confers titles, and yet last year, at the instance of the Prime Minister, he voted for a resolution ratifying an Order in Council that distinctly and emphatically declared that the King no longer should confer honours except on the advice or his ministers. In other words-

Might II correct my hon. friend? I said " the King surrounded by his constitutional advisers," and I do not want those words left out.
Mr. NI'CKLE: It makes very little difference which way the hon. gentleman puts it. I am quite willing to take it as he now expresses it. If he puts it that way the loyalty cry is exploded and gone.
Now I come to the question of foreign titles, which came before the Committee in this way. I, as Chairman of the Committee, received from (the President of the Privy Council this letter:-
Dear Mr. Nickle,-
By direction of Council I enclose herewith a copy of a communication from the Secretary of State with certain enclosures relating (to titles. It raises the question of residents in Canada accepting: titles from other sovereigns.
There was also enclosed another letter from the Under Secretary of State to the President of the Privy Council, directing the attention of the President of the Privy Council to the fact that a foreign dignitary had offered a title to a Canadian citizen, and the opinion of the committee was requested in reference to the matter. Now, what happened was this. One of the members raised a point of order, that consideration of that question was out of order. But the fact that the matter had been referred to the committee by the President of the Privy Council, and that the reference read this way, made the chairman reach the conclusion that the matter was not out of order. Here was the reference:
It referred to the committee various things, together with the question of conferring hon-

ours, titular distinctions and decoration^ upon subjects of His Majesty ordinarily resident in Canada, including those who had performed overseas, in Canada or elsewhere naval, military and civilian services in connection with the war.
In the resolution there was no limitation as to the conferring of titles being restricted to British titles, and it was therefore ruled that the matter could be discussed by the committee. What was the result?
On motion of Mr. Cockshutt it was resolved that inasmuch as this committee has decided to recommend that no further titles or orders be conferred by His Majesty the King on Canadians. the committee is opposed to the acceptance by Canadians of titles or orders from foreign rulers or governments.
And yet the member for Brantford stands in his place to-night and says that he is prepared to vote for an amendment that negatives the very resolution that he prepared in the committee. O! consistency, thou art a jewel.
Go for it.

And the member for
Brantford jocularly spoke of the wedding guest clothed in luxuriant wedding attire. But I wish to draw attention to the fact that the gentleman who was clothed in wedding attire always wears his attire on State occasions while the member for Brantford appears similarly attired on all occasions.
Now, Sir, I want to go further-and I must speak quickly because it is getting late.
Go for it.

The member for Algoma directed my attention to a few things, particularly to the irregularity, as he saw it, of the words, "professional or vocational character or which appertain to an office," being used in suibclause (a) of the first paragraph of the report. Let us see what is meant and decide if this report is or is not regular. Does the member for Algoma know that when a lieutenancy is given to a man and he gets his commission, it is issued in His Majesty's name? Does he know that when a man is appointed a notary public for the purpose of taking oaths his commission is issued under the name of His Majesty? Does he know that when a man is appointed to any judicial position his commission is issued under His Majesty's name? In the name of common sense how are you going to make an exception unless you use language to express your idea? The committee was perfectly consistent in the report. Let me
read it to the House. !I leave out the preamble :	'
We, Your IJajesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the House of Commons of Canada in Parliament assembled, huimbly approach Your Majesty-
And in passing may I suggest to you, Sir, that I do not see anything in the nature of a demand when you say that you humbly approach His Majesty.
-praying that Your Majesty may be graciously pleased:-
(a) To refrain hereafter from conferring any title of honour or titular distinction upon any of your subjects domiciled or ordinarily resident in Canada, save such appellations as are of a professional or vocational character or which appertain to an office.
What does that mean in plain language? It simply means that the committee recommended to this House to pass an Address asking His Majesty to refrain from conferring titular distinctions on his subjects domiciled or living in Canada, but that that should not stop His Majesty from issuing commissions appertaining to such appointments as a lieutenancy, a notary public, or a judgeship. There is nothing out of the way in the reference; it is a sound and proper expression of an idea, and I am rather surprised that the member for East Algoma took the position that he did tonight.
I wish to revert for a moment to the member for Brantford; I cannot leave him altogether without a few remarks. He professes to speak for his constituency, and, if I understood him aright, he endeavoured to lead the House to the conclusion that his people were not interested. I hold in any hand a telegram addressed to the Chairman of the Titles Committee, Ottawa; as follows:
Resolved that this Brantford trades and labour council strongly resent the attitude of W. P. Cockshutt in the granting of Imperial titles to Canadian citizens and repudiate the insinuation that Brantford workingmen were not opposed to the same. The above council represents 1,487 Unionists.
A. G. Brown,
President.
I leave it to you, Mr. Speaker, and to this House to decide just who speaks for the riding of Brantford.
When my attention was first directed to what I considered a wrong in this country, I determined, if my weak efforts would bring about a reformation, to do what I could .to secure a reform. I brought the question into the House last year in reference to hereditary titles. I stated at that time that if an amendment were moved

and if I .thought the sentiment of the people warranted it, I would support a resolution to do away with all titular distinctions. The Prime Minister took the position last year that as the Government had stated its policy in an Order in Council, he was not prepared to go further than the Order in Council went; and the inevitable happened-the House sustained the Prime Minister. This year I again introduced the subject; and I told you at the beginning of my few remarks just what happened when the matter was discussed in this House on the 14th of April. I said that evening that I had approached this matter with sincerity; that I wanted results, not notoriety. I am just as sincere in the advocacy of the principles that I am enunciating here as other men are in their advocacy of principles on the floor of this 'House, and I expect from them exactly what I am prepared to accord to them-recognition of my good faith, and of my desire at least to carry out a reform as I see it. As I have said, a gulf lies between the position taken by myself and those who support me and the position taken by the member for South Toronto (Mr. Sheard). I believe that the granting of these titular distinctions is pernicious, and that it has a bad national effect. The member for South Toronto says: You are wrong; the principle is all right; it is the method employed in granting these distinctions that has brought about the grievance you decry. This House to-night has to decide which way it is going. It bas to make a decision that will probably regulate and influence our national life for the next fifty years, because if the House decides in accordance with the amendment moved by the member for East Algoma, the probabilities are that there will he such a flood of titles that the flood-gates, once opened, cannot be closed for years.. There is no use in trying to camouflage the issue; it is clear-cut and well defined. The issue before the House and the country to-night is this:	Is the Parliament of Canada in
favour of titles and titular distinctions being granted to Canadians? You cannot hide this thing any longer under a veil of mystery. The question that has to be decided is this:	Are you in favour of
giving to any Government the right, to denominate who shall have titular distinction? If you are, vote for the amendment submitted by the member for East Algoma. If, on the other hand, the members of this House are consistent in standing by the principles that they have enunciated 
in times past, then I ask them to stand by the report of the Committee. In my judgment, that report honestly expresses the intention of the Committee, honestly expresses the wishes of the people; and its adoption will be not only a step forward, but also the attainment of a goal in doing aw.ay, once and for all with a pernicious principle in this country. If this report is. adopted Canada will take the position she should take-that, being' a true democracy, she is opposed to priorities and personal recognitions and declare that all men are equal and that what is good enough for one man is good enough for all.
